description: Aphelion - X brings NASA’s SPHEREx infrared sky survey to life. Search for a star or select a region of the sky, then compare observations over time with an interactive blink viewer. Watch moving objects and changing stars stand out, explore their infrared colours, and understand what the data reveals. Designed for curious learners and citizen scientists, Xsphere makes astronomical data accessible through visual exploration, motion tracking, and shareable views of our changing universe.
summary:
SPHEREx Blink is a free web tool that turns NASA's SPHEREx infrared survey into short sky videos. Type any star's name (typos are fine) or any RA/Dec, or draw a box on the sky, and the tool fetches every SPHEREx photo of that patch, groups them into visits, stacks each visit into one clean frame and plays them as a blink. Moving objects such as nearby stars and brown dwarfs, and changing ones such as variable stars, jump out.

It answers the challenge directly: enter coordinates, see the same patch at each SPHEREx epoch "like a little video". All five test targets play real SPHEREx blinks. It also adds a difference view, Short/Mid/Long wavelength groups built from the 102 bands, a spectrum on the fly, a light curve, Gaia and WISE overlays, contamination flags, and a "Detections" layer that marks moving, variable and shifted sources as candidates, checked against Gaia, WISE, 2MASS and known asteroids.

Why it matters: in 1930 a blink comparator found Pluto, and volunteers blinking WISE images have found many brown dwarfs. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months. Our tool lets anyone, from a single link, search it for the next nearby cold world.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Blink is a blink comparator for NASA's newest all-sky survey. It is the same idea Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto in 1930: flip between two photos of the same sky and look for the dot that jumped. SPHEREx photographs the entire sky about every six months in 102 infrared colours. That is far too much to flip through by hand, so our tool does the fetching, aligning and comparing, and leaves the looking to people.

How it works, step by step

  • Find a spot. Type a star name or coordinates. Name lookup is typo-tolerant ("betelgeuze", "alphacentauri", "trappist 1" all work) and falls back to the CDS Sesame resolver for any catalogued object. For the test targets, positions are moved forward with proper motion to each photo's date, since catalogue positions of fast movers are arcminutes out of date.
  • Ask NASA which photos cover it. The engine queries IRSA's SPHEREx image search (SIA/TAP) for Level-2 images from the DR1 and QR3 releases, wide and deep surveys. If IRSA is down, it uses our own index built from the image headers in NASA's public S3 bucket.
  • Read only the patch. It reads just the needed pixels from the S3 bucket with byte-range requests, or uses the IRSA cutout service.
  • Group into visits. Photos are sorted by time; a gap of more than 60 days starts a new visit. Deep fields observed almost continuously (such as R Draconis near the north ecliptic pole) are split by calendar month.
  • Stack each visit. All photos of a visit are aligned on one north-up grid at SPHEREx's native 6.15″ per pixel and combined into one frame, per detector. Because SPHEREx uses a linear variable filter, every exposure sees the target at a different wavelength, so we never blink across different wavelengths. The 102 bands are grouped into Short, Mid and Long wavelength views.
  • Compare. Display modes: Blink, Difference (later visit minus the first, in units of noise), and Side by side. One brightness stretch is used for the whole sequence, so real changes are not hidden by per-frame scaling.
  • Detect and check. The "Detections" switch marks movers, variables and sources that shifted between visits. Movers must line up along a straight track over at least three visits. Every source is cross-matched against ESA Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020, AllWISE and 2MASS, and one-off spots are checked against known asteroids with IMCCE SkyBoT. Anything unexplained is labelled a candidate.
  • Second opinion from our ML model. Each detected source also gets a class (star, infrared-only, unmatched), a confidence and an "oddness" percentile from our own triage model, so users can sort by "check first". Trained on 9,427 catalogue-labelled SPHEREx sources in 43 zones: 93.1 % accuracy on held-out sky vs 65.7 % baseline.
  • See the photos and the star. When you select an area, the real outline of every SPHEREx photo covering it is drawn on the sky, one colour per visit. For stars, a "View in 3D" button shows an artist's impression built from measured temperature (from Gaia colour), size (from brightness and parallax), distance and motion, clearly labelled as not an image.
  • Measure. A spectrum is built on the fly, one point per exposure at its own wavelength, and a light curve shows brightness at every visit. Pixels with quality problems are flagged from the SPHEREx contamination flags.
  • Share. Coordinates live in the URL, a share panel copies the link, and an /embed version drops the view into any web page.
  • Stay current. A weekly job asks NASA again for every cached spot and rebuilds it if new photos exist. The five test targets are pre-loaded so they open fast.

Does it work? All five test targets play real SPHEREx blinks. On Barnard's Star the engine measures a motion of about 10.2″ per year, close to the 10.4″ per year from Gaia DR3. ε Indi B and WISE 0855−0714 are also recovered as movers and matched to Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020. WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is invisible at short wavelengths and appears in the long-wavelength view, as expected for an object that cold. R Draconis and RW Aurigae show up as variables. Tests with fake movers injected into real data show recovery is good above about one SPHEREx pixel per year and weak below it: an honest limit of a roughly one-year baseline, which grows with every release.

Benefits

Anyone can explore NASA's newest survey without software or archive queries. Students see proper motion, variability and infrared colour with their own eyes; citizen scientists get a fast first look at any patch with known stars and asteroids already filtered out; astronomers get shareable links and an open pipeline.

What we hope to achieve

A public inbox where volunteers review and vote on candidates, like the Backyard Worlds project did for WISE; a stronger version of our triage model with brown-dwarf and variable-star classes; and longer baselines as SPHEREx keeps surveying, which will reach slower and fainter movers.

Tools and languages

Python 3.11 (Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, reproject, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, FastAPI) for the engine and model; TypeScript and React with Vite for the web app; Aladin Lite (CDS) for the interactive sky map; three.js for the 3D star impressions; a Linux VPS with Caddy for hosting. The engine is also exposed as an MCP server, so AI assistants can call the same tools.

How we cover the challenge

  • Public web tool, enter RA/Dec, see images change over time "like a little video" → Search by name or RA/Dec, Blink mode, visit timeline
  • Test on Barnard's Star, ε Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis → All five play real SPHEREx blinks; pre-loaded; one-click test-target chips
  • Optional: easy to update with new releases → Releases listed in one config file; weekly data-update job; only new photos are downloaded
  • Optional: creative use of the 102 bands, co-add detectors for signal → Per-detector stacking; Short/Mid/Long wavelength groups
  • Optional "extra kudos": spectra on the fly → Spectrum built live, one point per exposure at its own wavelength
  • Optional: add or subtract epochs → Difference mode (later visit minus first)
  • Optional: user-chosen field of view → Area selection: draw a box of any size on the sky, with the photo footprints drawn per visit
  • Optional: Gaia / WISE overlays → Gaia and WISE overlays; cross-match in Detections
  • Optional: coordinates in the URL, embeddable → Coordinates in the URL, share panel, /embed
  • Optional: metadata such as contamination flags → SPHEREx quality and contamination flags shown on the frame
  • Optional: use Astropy and Aladin → Astropy throughout the engine; Aladin Lite for the sky map
  • Model on WiseView → Same blink-and-compare workflow, for SPHEREx
